question: Two nodes v1,v2 have nodal equations 3v1−v2=5 and −v1+2v2=0, with currents in mA and conductances in mS. Find v1 in volts.

steps: The second equation gives v2=v1/2.
Substitute into the first: (3−1/2)v1=5.
Thus 2.5v1=5 and v1=2 V; v2=1 V also satisfies both equations.
solution.explanation: Thus 2.5v1=5 and v1=2 V; v2=1 V also satisfies both equations.
commonMistakes: Use simultaneous node equations; grounding the second node changes the circuit.

question: Under the passive sign convention, a load has RMS phasors V=10∠0° V and I=2∠−60° A. Find its average absorbed power in watts.

steps: The current is conjugated in complex power, giving phase +60°.
The apparent-power magnitude is 10×2=20 VA.
Its real part is 20cos60°=10 W.
commonMistakes: RMS phasors do not require a further factor 1/2.

hints: Identify the conditions under which complex power applies.
Start from $ S=V_{rms}I_{rms}^*,\quad P=VI\cos\phi $.

question: A delta network has each side 9 Ω. Find each resistance in its equivalent balanced star in ohms.

steps: Each star arm is the product of its two adjoining delta sides divided by the sum of all three sides.
Here that is 9×9/(9+9+9).
The result is 81/27=3 Ω.
commonMistakes: For a balanced network the delta resistance is three times a star arm.

hints: Identify the conditions under which delta-to-star conversion applies.
Start from $ R_Y=R_\Delta^2/(3R_\Delta) $.

verification.method: Delta-to-star product/sum formula; equal-terminal equivalent resistance checked. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: A causal continuous-time signal has Laplace transform X(s)=1/[(s+1)(s+3)]. Find x(0+).

steps: There is no impulse term because X is strictly proper with denominator degree 2.
The ratio tends to zero, so x(0+)=0.
solution.explanation: The ratio tends to zero, so x(0+)=0.
commonMistakes: Apply the initial-value theorem only after checking that an impulse does not make the ordinary value undefined.

question: A two-tap FIR filter is y[n]=x[n]−x[n−1]. Find |H(eʲΩ)| at Ω=π/2.

steps: At Ω=π/2 the delayed exponential is −j.
Thus H=1+j.
Its magnitude is √(1²+1²)=√2≈1.414213562.
commonMistakes: Do not subtract magnitudes before combining complex contributions.

hints: Identify the conditions under which discrete-time frequency response applies.
Start from $ H(e^{j\Omega})=1-e^{-j\Omega} $.

question: The 4-point DFT uses X[k]=Σₙ₌₀³x[n]exp(−j2πkn/4). For x=[1,0,−1,0], find the real part of X[1].

steps: Only n=0 and n=2 contribute.
At k=1 their terms are 1 and (−1)e⁻ʲπ=1.
X[1]=2, purely real.

options.text: z11 = z22 is required by reciprocity alone
An open-circuit output measurement is used to determine z11 and z21 from port-1 excitation

question: For x[n]=(1/3)ⁿu[n], find the radius of the inner boundary of the causal bilateral z-transform ROC.

solution.asked: Find the pole magnitude bounding the causal ROC.
steps: The geometric series converges when |1/(3z)|<1.
This is equivalent to |z|>1/3.
The inner-boundary radius is 1/3; the boundary itself is excluded.
solution.explanation: The inner-boundary radius is 1/3; the boundary itself is excluded.
commonMistakes: A rational expression alone does not specify the ROC or causality.

hints: Identify the conditions under which z-transform roc applies.
Start from $ X(z)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(1/(3z))^n $.

verification.method: Geometric-series ratio convergence boundary for causal z-transform. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: An initially charged RC circuit has v(0)=1 V, final voltage 4 V, and τ=2 s. Find v(2 ln3) in volts.

solution.asked: Find the response at the stated time.
steps: The initial deviation from the final state is 1−4=−3 V.
At t=2 ln3, the decay factor is 1/3.
The voltage is 4−3/3=3 V.
commonMistakes: Natural and forced response must combine to satisfy the nonzero initial state.

hints: Identify the conditions under which general first-order state transition applies.
Start from $ v(t)=v_\infty+(v_0-v_\infty)e^{-t/\tau} $.

verification.method: RK4 integration of charged-to-final RC differential equation. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.

question: For discrete-time causal FIR filters with a finite number of finite-valued taps, which statements hold?

options.text: Their impulse response is absolutely summable
Every such filter has a nonzero DC gain
Their output is a finite weighted sum of present/past input samples

steps: A finite sum of finite tap magnitudes is finite, satisfying the LTI BIBO condition.
The causal convolution uses only present and previous input samples.
DC gain is the tap sum, which can be zero (for example [1,−1]). Select A, B and D.
solution.explanation: DC gain is the tap sum, which can be zero (for example [1,−1]). Select A, B and D.
commonMistakes: A stable filter can reject DC entirely.

hints: Identify the conditions under which fir support and summability applies.

question: A real sequence x=[1,2,3,4] has a 4-point DFT under the unnormalized forward convention. Find (1/4)Σₖ₌₀³|X[k]|².

steps: The DFT orthogonality makes the stated normalized spectral energy equal to time-domain energy.
Sum 1²+2²+3²+4².
The result is 1+4+9+16=30.
commonMistakes: Normalization depends on the DFT convention; the factor 1/4 is given.

hints: Identify the conditions under which dft parseval identity applies.
Start from $ \sum_n|x[n]|^2=\frac1N\sum_k|X[k]|^2 $.

verification.method: Compute every DFT bin and sum spectral magnitudes directly. Arithmetic checked by executable calculation/property fixtures; same-system solution review only.
